claims.text: Adding approximately 5–10 wt.% Mo to the surface boride layer will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Mo doping will promote formation of a Mo-enriched passive layer in the boride-based coating.
The Mo-enriched layer may contain Mo-boride complexes.
The Mo-enriched interfacial layer will be stable and less reactive than the untreated boride matrix.
Mo incorporation alters the electronic properties of the boride coating.
Mo incorporation alters the phase stability of the boride coating.
These changes reduce the coating's chemical reactivity with molten aluminum.
A Mo-associated protective surface film can limit pitting corrosion.
The Mo-enriched passive film will decrease dissolution during exposure to molten aluminum.
Relative to untreated boride-based components, Mo-doped samples will have lower weight loss during molten-aluminum exposure.
Relative to untreated boride-based components, Mo-doped samples will have lower corrosion-pit density during molten-aluminum exposure.
Relative to untreated boride-based components, Mo-doped samples will exhibit improved overall surface stability in molten aluminum.
The protective effect should remain effective at approximately 660–700 °C for exposure durations typical of hot-dip aluminum plating.
Ambient oxygen that permits minor passivation is a condition for the proposed effect.
Temperatures or exposure times substantially above typical operating conditions may diminish the protective effect.
Mo concentrations substantially outside the proposed optimal range may diminish the protective effect.
The optimal Mo concentration and the passive layer's long-term stability under cyclic thermal and chemical exposure are uncertain.
